source.title: Learn Any Skill Fast
source.attribution: A Reborn guide in our own words, drawing on Josh Kaufman's The First 20 Hours, research on deliberate practice, and the testing and spacing effects.
source.notes: Written by Reborn in our own words; no text copied. References: Pablo Stafforini, Summary of The First 20 Hours by Josh Kaufman, https://stafforini.com/notes/summary-of-the-first-20-hours-by-josh-kaufman/; Wikipedia, Practice (learning method), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Practice_(learning_method); Wikipedia, Testing effect, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Testing_effect; Wikipedia, Spaced repetition, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaced_repetition

cards.title: Pick one skill and decide what good enough looks like
cards.body:
Trying to learn guitar, coding and a new language all at once usually means making little progress in any of them. Choose one skill you're genuinely excited about and give it your focus for a few weeks.

Then define your target. Mastery takes years, but you rarely need it. What does good enough mean for you? 'Play five songs to sing along with friends.' 'Hold a ten-minute conversation in Spanish.' 'Build a simple website for my shop.'

A clear, specific target tells you what to practise and what to ignore. It also tells you when you've succeeded, which keeps motivation high. Vague goals like 'get better at cooking' give you nothing to aim at.
cards.apply_it: Write one sentence: 'I want to be able to ... by ...' for the skill you most want to learn.

quiz.question: Which is the most useful learning target?
options: Get better at the piano
Play three simple songs from memory in six weeks
Become a world-class pianist
Learn music somehow
quiz.explanation: A specific, realistic target shows you what to practise and when you have succeeded.

cards.title: Break the skill into small parts and find the few that matter most
cards.body:
Most skills are really bundles of smaller skills. Cooking involves knife work, heat control, seasoning and timing. Public speaking involves structure, voice, eye contact and handling nerves.

List the parts of your skill. Then ask: which few parts give the biggest results for my goal? Often a small number of sub-skills do most of the work. A beginner guitarist who learns four common chords can already play many songs.

Practise those core parts first and leave the rest for later. Breaking a skill down also makes it less scary. 'Learn to swim' feels huge; 'learn to float on my back' feels doable today.
cards.apply_it: List five sub-skills of your chosen skill and circle the two that matter most for your goal.

quiz.question: Why break a skill into sub-skills?
options: To make it take longer
So you can skip practising
To practise the most important parts first
To avoid setting a goal
quiz.explanation: A few core sub-skills often deliver most of the results, so focusing on them speeds progress.

cards.title: Learn just enough to start practising and correct yourself
cards.body:
A common trap is reading book after book or watching endless videos before ever trying the skill. Research feels productive, but it can become a way of putting off the uncomfortable part: actually doing it.

Instead, gather three or four good sources, such as a beginner's book, a well-reviewed course or a few trusted videos. Skim them to learn the basics and the most common mistakes. Your aim is to know enough to notice when you are doing something wrong, so you can fix it as you go.

Then start practising. You'll learn far more from trying, failing and adjusting than from more reading. Return to your sources when you hit a specific question.
cards.apply_it: Pick three beginner resources for your skill and spend no more than an hour skimming them before your first practice.

quiz.question: How much should you research before starting to practise?
options: Enough to spot and fix your own mistakes
Nothing; just guess
Everything available, before trying at all
Only what a friend tells you
quiz.explanation: Learning just enough to self-correct gets you practising sooner, where most learning happens.

cards.title: Remove the barriers that stop you practising
cards.body:
Often the hardest part of learning isn't the skill itself but getting started each day. Small barriers add up: the guitar is in its case in a cupboard, the running shoes are lost, the phone keeps buzzing.

Make practice as easy as possible. Get the tools you need before you begin. Keep them where you'll see them. Turn off notifications and tell people you're busy for twenty minutes.

There are emotional barriers too: fear of looking silly, or of being bad at first. Name them honestly. Everyone is clumsy at the start, and that's not a sign you lack talent. It's simply what the beginning of learning feels like.
cards.apply_it: Set up your practice space tonight so you can start tomorrow's session within one minute.

quiz.question: Which of these is a practical way to remove a barrier to practice?
options: Keep your equipment out and ready to use
Wait until you feel fully motivated
Practise only when you have a whole free day
quiz.explanation: Making practice easy to start cuts the friction that often stops people before they begin.

cards.title: Practise deliberately, just beyond what feels easy
cards.body:
Repeating what you can already do feels pleasant but teaches you little. Researchers who study experts found that what matters most is how you practise, not just how long. They call it deliberate practice.

Deliberate practice means picking one specific thing to improve, working on it with full attention, and pushing slightly beyond your comfort zone. A pianist might play one difficult bar slowly ten times rather than the whole piece again. A speaker might rehearse just their opening.

It is effortful and sometimes frustrating, which is a sign it's working. Aim for good form first, then build speed. Rushing with poor technique just practises your mistakes.
cards.apply_it: In your next session, choose one weak spot and spend ten focused minutes on only that.

quiz.question: What is deliberate practice?
options: Repeating what you already do well
Practising for as many hours as possible without a plan
Focused work on a specific weakness, just beyond your comfort zone
Watching others perform
quiz.explanation: Targeted, effortful work on specific weaknesses drives improvement far more than easy repetition.

cards.title: Get fast, honest feedback on how you're doing
cards.body:
You can't fix what you can't see. Feedback shows you what's working and what isn't, so you can adjust before bad habits set in.

The best feedback is quick and specific. A coach or teacher is ideal if you can find one. If not, there are many free options: record yourself speaking or playing and listen back, compare your work with a good example, use apps or exercises that mark your answers, or ask a skilled friend to watch for five minutes.

Try not to take criticism personally. Feedback is information, not a judgement of your worth. Ask for one or two things to improve at a time, rather than a long list.
cards.apply_it: Record yourself doing the skill for two minutes today, then watch or listen back and note one thing to improve.

quiz.question: What makes feedback most useful for learning?
options: It is quick and specific
It comes months later
It only praises you
It covers every possible fault at once
quiz.explanation: Fast, specific feedback lets you correct mistakes before they become habits.

cards.title: Practise in short sessions, most days
cards.body:
You don't need long, exhausting sessions to make progress. Short, focused practice done regularly usually beats occasional marathons. Twenty to forty-five minutes a day, or even several ten-minute bursts, can move you forward quickly.

Short sessions are easier to fit into a busy life, so you're more likely to stick with them. They also help your brain consolidate what you've learned between sessions, especially when you sleep.

Schedule your practice like an appointment rather than waiting for spare time to appear, because it rarely does. Using a timer helps too: set it, give full attention until it rings, then stop. Ending while you still feel fresh makes you keener to come back tomorrow.
cards.apply_it: Put a daily twenty-minute practice slot in your calendar for the next seven days.

quiz.question: Which practice pattern tends to work best?
options: One five-hour session a month
Short, focused sessions most days
Practising only when you feel inspired
quiz.explanation: Regular short sessions are easier to keep up and give your brain time to consolidate learning.

cards.title: Commit to the first 20 hours to get past the awkward start
cards.body:
The beginning of any new skill feels awkward. You're slow, you make obvious mistakes, and it's tempting to decide you're just not good at it. This frustration is the main reason people quit.

Writer Josh Kaufman suggests committing in advance to about 20 hours of focused, deliberate practice. That's roughly 45 minutes a day for a month. It won't make you an expert, but it's often enough to go from knowing nothing to being reasonably good, enough to enjoy the skill and keep going.

Deciding ahead of time takes the daily question 'Should I quit?' off the table. You simply show up and put in the hours.
cards.apply_it: Make a simple tally chart of 20 boxes, one per hour of practice, and fill in your first box this week.

quiz.question: What is the main idea behind committing to the first 20 hours?
options: 20 hours makes you a world expert
Talent matters more than practice
You should stop after exactly 20 hours
Pre-committing helps you push through the frustrating early stage
quiz.explanation: Committing in advance helps you get past the awkward start to a useful, enjoyable level.

cards.title: Test yourself and space out your reviews to remember more
cards.body:
When a skill involves knowledge, like vocabulary, chords, formulas or rules, how you review matters. Rereading notes feels easy but doesn't stick well. Pulling information out of your memory, by testing yourself, makes it much stronger. This is called retrieval practice.

Spacing helps too. Instead of cramming, review something a day later, then a few days later, then a week later. Each time you almost forget and then remember, the memory gets more durable. Flashcards and spaced-repetition apps make this easy.

Combine the two: cover your notes, try to recall or perform from memory, then check and correct. A bit of struggle is a sign your brain is working.
cards.apply_it: Make five flashcards on what you learned this week and test yourself tomorrow without looking first.

quiz.question: Which review method usually builds stronger memory?
options: Testing yourself, with reviews spread over days
Highlighting more of the textbook
Rereading notes several times in one night
Listening to notes while doing something else
quiz.explanation: Retrieval practice combined with spacing is one of the best-supported ways to remember.

cards.title: Learn from people who already have the skill
cards.body:
People who are good at your skill can save you months of trial and error. They know which parts matter, which mistakes are common and what progress really looks like.

Watch skilled performers closely and try to copy specific things: how a cook holds a knife, how a speaker pauses, how a coder names things. Ask experienced people a few focused questions, such as 'What do beginners usually get wrong?' or 'What would you practise if you started again?'

Their answers also help set realistic expectations, so you don't feel discouraged when progress is slower than you hoped. Many people enjoy helping a keen learner. Join a club, class or online community where you can ask and share.
cards.apply_it: Ask one person who is good at your skill: 'What do beginners most often get wrong?'

quiz.question: What is a great question to ask an expert when starting out?
options: Can you do it for me?
Is there a way to skip practice?
What do beginners usually get wrong?
quiz.explanation: Knowing the common mistakes helps you avoid them and focus your practice.

cards.title: Expect plateaus and push through them with small changes
cards.body:
Progress is rarely a straight line. After a fast start, most learners hit a plateau where they practise and nothing seems to improve. This is normal, not a sign you've reached your limit.

Plateaus often happen because practice has become comfortable and automatic. To break through, change something. Slow down and work on a weak spot. Try a harder piece or a new challenge. Get fresh feedback from someone more skilled. Sometimes rest helps too; skills can click after a short break.

It also helps to look back. Compare a recording from your first week with today. You've usually improved more than you feel. Celebrate that, then set your next small target.
cards.apply_it: If you feel stuck, change one thing in your practice this week: speed, difficulty or who gives you feedback.

quiz.question: What does a learning plateau usually mean?
options: You have reached your natural limit
Practice may have become too comfortable and needs changing
You should give up the skill
Feedback is no longer useful
quiz.explanation: Plateaus are normal and often break when you add challenge, feedback or variety.

cards.title: Teach what you learn to lock it in
cards.body:
One of the best ways to understand something deeply is to explain it to someone else. Teaching forces you to organise your thoughts, find simple words and notice the gaps in your own knowledge.

You don't need to be an expert to teach. Show a friend the three chords you've learned. Explain a new idea to a younger sibling. Write a short post about what you discovered this week. If you can't explain it simply, that tells you exactly what to review next.

Teaching also connects you with others who share your interest, which keeps you motivated. Learning becomes something you give, not just something you get, and that makes it more likely to last.
cards.apply_it: Explain one thing you learned this week to someone else in under two minutes.

quiz.question: Why does teaching others help you learn?
options: It shows off your knowledge
It means you can stop practising
Only experts benefit from teaching
It forces you to organise ideas and reveals gaps
quiz.explanation: Explaining something simply exposes what you don't yet understand, so you know what to review.
